# Lichen planus

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Dermatology > Idiopathic disorders > Lichen planus*

[Original Article Link](/library/5k0ioT)

---

## Summary

Lichen planus is a chronic inflammatory disease characterized by lesions involving the <u>skin</u> (i.e., cutaneous), <u>mucosa</u> (i.e., <u>mucosal</u>), and <u>hair</u> or <u>nails</u> (i.e., appendageal). It most commonly affects adults aged 30–60 years. The exact etiology is unknown. <u>Cutaneous lichen planus</u> typically manifests as pruritic purple <u>papules</u> and <u>plaques</u> with well-demarcated irregular borders and <u>Wickham striae</u> on the extremities (e.g., wrists and ankles). <u>Mucosal lichen planus</u> manifestations include <u>papules</u>, <u>plaques</u>, <u>Wickham striae</u>, and <u>erosions</u> on the oral, esophageal, and/or genital <u>mucosa</u>. Diagnosis is based on the presence of clinical features or typical <u>histology</u>; <u>biopsy</u> should be performed if the diagnosis is uncertain. <u>Screening for hepatitis C</u> should be considered for all patients. Early specialist consult is required for <u>mucosal lichen planus</u> and <u>hypertrophic cutaneous lichen planus</u> because of the risk of treatment resistance and the potential for malignant transformation to <u>squamous cell carcinoma</u> (<u>SCC</u>). First-line treatment consists of <u>high-potency topical steroids</u>; intralesional preparations are indicated for <u>hypertrophic</u> cutaneous disease and appendageal involvement.

---

## Epidemiology

* <u>Prevalence</u>: rare disease (occurs in < 1% of the population) [[1]](/library/RJXlF_)[[2]](/library/Ugdbu60)

* Age of onset: 30–60 years [[3]](/library/QJXuF_)

* Sex [[1]](/library/RJXlF_)

* <u>Cutaneous lichen planus</u>: ♀=♂

* Oral lichen planus is more common in women




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

Although the exact etiology of lichen planus is unknown, possible etiologic factors include:




* Altered <u>immune response</u> with <u>T cell</u> activation  [[4]](/library/M9bMLD)[[5]](/library/PJXW8_)

* Associated with <u>hepatitis C infections</u> [[6]](/library/4JX38_)

---

## Clinical features

Lichen planus is categorized based on the areas of involvement: cutaneous, <u>mucosal</u>, and appendageal. The most common cutaneous and <u>mucosal</u> manifestations are presented here. Additional manifestations are described in “Subtypes and variants.” [[1]](/library/RJXlF_)




### Cutaneous lichen planus [[2]](/library/Ugdbu60)[[7]](/library/PhdWVp0)




* 6 Ps of cutaneous lichen planus 

* Purple (violaceous)

* Polygonal, irregular borders

* Planar (flat-topped)

* Pruritic, often severe

* <u>Papules</u>

* <u>Plaques</u>

* Wickham striae: white reticular lines on the surface of the lesions

* Bilateral, symmetrical involvement of the extremities (e.g., ankles, flexor wrists) and, in some cases, the trunk

* Lesions are arranged in linear or circular groups that may coalesce into larger <u>plaques</u>.

* <u>Koebner phenomenon</u>

* See also <u>hypertrophic cutaneous lichen planus</u> in “Subtypes and variants.”

### Mucosal lichen planus [[2]](/library/Ugdbu60)[[7]](/library/PhdWVp0)




See “Subtypes and variants” for information on esophageal lichen planus.




* Oral lichen planus  [[1]](/library/RJXlF_)[[7]](/library/PhdWVp0)[[8]](/library/shdt2p0)

* Affects the buccal <u>mucosa</u>, <u>gingiva</u>, and <u>tongue</u>

* Reticular type: <u>Wickham striae</u>, asymptomatic

* <u>Erythematous</u> type: <u>atrophic</u> <u>erythematous</u> <u>plaques</u>

* Erosive type: <u>erosions</u> associated with <u>pain</u> and a burning sensation

* Genital lichen planus 

* All patients

* <u>Papules</u>, <u>Wickham striae</u>, and, if severe, scarring and adhesions

* <u>Pruritus</u>, a burning sensation, or <u>dyspareunia</u> may be present.

* Male genitalia: annular lesions on the <u>glans penis</u> and coronal sulcus [[9]](/library/Njd-0J0)

* Female genitalia: <u>erosions</u> on the labia, <u>clitoris</u>, and <u>vagina</u> [[10]](/library/onW08N0)

> [!TIP]
> <u>Postinflammatory hypopigmentation</u> and <u>postinflammatory hyperpigmentation</u> may be present. [[1]](/library/RJXlF_)

## Subtypes and variants

### Hypertrophic cutaneous lichen planus [[2]](/library/Ugdbu60)[[7]](/library/PhdWVp0)




* A subtype of <u>cutaneous lichen planus</u>; also called <u>lichen planus verrucosus</u>

* Scaly; , <u>hyperkeratotic</u>, <u>verrucous</u> <u>plaques</u> and <u>nodules</u>

* Predominantly affect the shins, ankles, and <u>interphalangeal joints</u>

* Severely pruritic





### Esophageal lichen planus [[7]](/library/PhdWVp0)




* A subtype of <u>mucosal lichen planus</u>

* Symptoms: <u>dysphagia</u>, <u>odynophagia</u>

* Endoscopic findings: strictures, <u>papules</u> with <u>Wickham striae</u>, <u>erosions</u>, sloughing, stenosis [[11]](/library/6NdjXq0)





### Appendegeal lichen planus [[7]](/library/PhdWVp0)




#### Lichen planopilaris [[7]](/library/PhdWVp0)




* Mainly affects the scalp of <u>postmenopausal</u> women and presents with <u>pruritus</u>, <u>hair</u> loss

* <u>Frontal fibrosing alopecia</u> (a variant of <u>lichen planopilaris</u>)

* Affects the scalp with <u>scarring alopecia</u>

* <u>Histology</u>: <u>hair follicles</u> are surrounded by a bandlike <u>lymphocytic</u> infiltrate

* <u>Direct immunofluorescence</u> shows subepidermal colloid bodies





![Lichen planopilaris](media/u1u1gcxco843418fmz042dw1.jpg)

Lichen planopilaris




#### <u>Nail</u> lichen planus [[7]](/library/PhdWVp0)




* A type of appendageal lichen planus

* <u>Nail</u> features

* Thinning, <u>atrophy</u>, <u>onycholysis</u>, longitudinal ridging

* Subungual <u>hyperkeratosis</u>

* Discoloration (e.g., yellow)

---

## Diagnosis

Lichen planus is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>. Diagnostic studies are indicated in patients with atypical, extensive, or refractory lesions. [[2]](/library/Ugdbu60)[[7]](/library/PhdWVp0)




* <u>Dermoscopy</u>:  to improve visualization of lesions (e.g., <u>Wickham striae</u>), especially in individuals with darker <u>skin</u>

* <u>Biopsy</u>:  to exclude differential diagnoses and <u>malignancy</u>; see “Pathology” for histopathologic findings   [[12]](/library/kmdmfq0)

* Endoscopy for symptoms of esophageal involvement

* <u>Laboratory studies</u>: Consider <u>HCV screening</u>, especially in individuals with <u>risk factors for HCV infection</u>. [[1]](/library/RJXlF_)[[2]](/library/Ugdbu60)





> [!TIP]
> Perform a history and <u>physical examination</u> to assess all potential areas of involvement (i.e., cutaneous, <u>mucosal</u>, appendageal). [[7]](/library/PhdWVp0)

---

## Pathology

* <u>Hyperkeratosis</u>

* Wedge-shaped <u>hypergranulosis</u> [[13]](/library/UHabpN)

* Irregular <u>acanthosis</u> (saw-<u>tooth</u> appearance) [[13]](/library/UHabpN)

* Band-like <u>lymphocytic</u> infiltrate at the <u>dermal-epidermal junction</u> [[14]](/library/2HaTpN)

## Differential diagnoses

* <u>Skin</u> lesions [[2]](/library/Ugdbu60)

* Drug-induced lichen planus (<u>lichenoid drug eruption</u>) [[1]](/library/RJXlF_)[[7]](/library/PhdWVp0)

* A dermatologic condition triggered by certain medications (e.g., <u>beta blockers</u>, <u>ACE inhibitors</u>, penicillamines, <u>thiazide diuretics</u>, <u>hydroxychloroquine</u>)

* Manifests with diffuse lesions that closely resemble lichen planus but are not histologically identical

* Management includes topical <u>glucocorticoids</u> and discontinuation of the causative medication.

* <u>Eczema</u>

* <u>Psoriasis</u> (<u>guttate psoriasis</u> and <u>plaque psoriasis</u>)

* <u>Lichen simplex chronicus</u>

* <u>Pityriasis rosea</u>

* <u>Prurigo nodularis</u>

* See also “<u>Maculopapular rash</u>” and “<u>Differential diagnosis of scaling</u>.”

* Oral lesions [[2]](/library/Ugdbu60)

* <u>Oral thrush</u>

* <u>Leukoplakia</u>

* Bite trauma to buccal <u>mucosa</u>

* <u>Genital lesions</u> [[7]](/library/PhdWVp0)[[9]](/library/Njd-0J0)

* <u>Lichen sclerosus</u>

* <u>Lichen simplex chronicus</u>

* <u>Squamous cell carcinoma</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Chronic graft-versus-host disease</u> can manifest with cutaneous and <u>mucosal</u> lesions that resemble lichen planus. [[15]](/library/qNdCXq0)




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

### <u>Cutaneous lichen planus</u> (non-<u>hypertrophic</u>) [[1]](/library/RJXlF_)[[2]](/library/Ugdbu60)[[7]](/library/PhdWVp0)




* High-<u>potency</u> or <u>ultra-high potency topical steroid</u> (first-line), e.g., <u>clobetasol</u> DOSAGE

* Oral <u>antihistamines</u>, e.g., <u>hydroxyzine</u>DOSAGE, as needed for <u>pruritus</u>.

* Reassess after 1–3 months; adjust treatment based on clinical response.  [[1]](/library/RJXlF_)[[10]](/library/onW08N0)

* For patients with refractory disease, refer to dermatology for <u>biopsy</u> and advanced treatments.

* Oral <u>steroids</u>, e.g., <u>prednisone</u> (<u>off-label</u>)DOSAGE

* <u>Phototherapy</u> (<u>UVB</u> and <u>PUVA</u>)

* Oral <u>retinoids</u> (e.g., acitretin)

* <u>Topical calcineurin inhibitors</u> (e.g., <u>pimecrolimus</u>, <u>tacrolimus</u>)

* <u>Methotrexate</u>

* Novel therapies: <u>JAK inhibitors</u>, <u>PDE-4 inhibitors</u>, <u>biologic immunomodulators</u> (e.g., <u>interleukin</u> inhibitors)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Topical calcineurin inhibitors</u> are associated with a theoretical risk of <u>malignancy</u> and must be used with caution, particularly in <u>mucosal</u> and <u>hypertrophic cutaneous lichen planus</u>. [[8]](/library/shdt2p0)




### <u>Hypertrophic</u> or noncutaneous lichen planus [[1]](/library/RJXlF_)[[2]](/library/Ugdbu60)[[7]](/library/PhdWVp0)[[8]](/library/shdt2p0)




Refer to appropriate specialists (e.g., dermatology, oral <u>surgery</u>, urology, gynecology) for management and long-term monitoring for complications (e.g., scarring, <u>SCC</u>). [[7]](/library/PhdWVp0)[[8]](/library/shdt2p0)[[10]](/library/onW08N0)




* <u>Glucocorticoids</u>

* <u>Mucosal lichen planus</u> flares (e.g., painful <u>erosions</u>): <u>off-label use</u> of topical or oral <u>steroids</u>

* Appendageal and <u>hypertrophic cutaneous lichen planus</u>: intralesional <u>glucocorticoids</u>

* Adjunctive treatments for symptomatic relief

* <u>Pruritus</u>: <u>hydroxyzine</u> DOSAGE

* Oral <u>pain</u>: <u>lidocaine mouthwash</u>

* <u>Dyspareunia</u>: water-based lubricants

* Prevention of complications

* Oral hygiene and <u>smoking cessation</u>  [[8]](/library/shdt2p0)

* <u>Foreskin hygiene</u> or vaginal dilators

* Advanced treatments for refractory disease or complications

* Advanced treatments are similar to those used for refractory <u>cutaneous lichen planus</u>.

* <u>Surgery</u> or dilatation may be needed for <u>mucosal</u> scarring, adhesions, or stenosis.





> [!TIP]
> Treatment is generally not indicated for asymptomatic <u>mucosal lichen planus</u>; reserve treatment for symptomatic flares (e.g., painful <u>erosions</u>). [[8]](/library/shdt2p0)




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Mucosal</u>, <u>hypertrophic</u> cutaneous, and appendageal lichen planus are associated with malignant transformation to <u>squamous cell carcinoma</u>. [[7]](/library/PhdWVp0)

---

## Prognosis

Any localization of erosive lichen planus can cause scarring, which may lead to functional limitations.




* <u>Cutaneous lichen planus</u>

* Usually <u>self-limited</u> (typically resolves within 1 year)  [[1]](/library/RJXlF_)

* Can cause lasting <u>hypopigmentation</u> and/or <u>hyperpigmentation</u>

* Oral lichen planus

* Chronic condition

* Potential for malignant transformation into <u>squamous cell carcinoma</u>

* <u>Genital lichen planus</u>: may lead to scarring and/or <u>synechiae</u> formation
